rationale: This qualitative political-economy case study of urban water governance in Ghana (synthesizing historical/policy documents and secondary survey/water-quality studies) centers on regulatory_model_ownership—specifically the corporatization of GWSC into GWCL, PPP reform trajectories (affermage vs. the 2005-2011 AVRL management contract), independent regulation under the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission Act (Act 538 of 1997), and potential 'public-people partnership' alternatives, alongside secondary discussion of ERP user-fee/subsidy reforms, rural-urban institutional decoupling, and NGO/community self-help participation. On the outcome side, the paper explicitly evaluates 'wide' versus 'deep' access across multiple co-central outcome families: effective_access (microbial/chemical water quality, supply intermittency/reliability, and per-capita daily water quantity, which receives the most extensive analytical attention), economic_access (household water expenditure shares of 9-15% and informal tanker prices 12x official tariffs), and primary_connection (overall coverage vs. inequitable piped-connection distribution across neighbourhoods and income quintiles), warranting primary_outcome_family = effective_access and assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple = multiple.
